newsitem.title: USA: Pathfinder spacecraft makes historic Mars landing.
newsitem.headline: Pathfinder spacecraft makes historic Mars landing.

text.p: The Pathfinder spacecraft made a historic safe landing on Mars on Friday and surprised scientists by transmitting signals they were not expecting to hear until much later in the day.

The radio signals told mission control at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena that the craft was in a stable condition on the ground with its revolutionary airbags deflated as planned and its three unfolding steel and graphite units planted firmly on Martian soil.

The landing set the stage for an unprecedented exploration of the Red Planet by a dune-buggy type vehicle called the "Mars rover," which will be driven by remote control from Earth as it conducts a one-week survey to chart the composition and size of Martian rocks, dust and debris.
President Bill Clinton hailed the landing and said, "Our return to Mars today marks the beginning of a new era in the nation's space exploration programme."

Scientists had not expected to hear from the spacecraft for four hours after its landing because Earth's position relative to Mars made the chance of getting signals remote. But shortly after the landing -- the first by a U.S. spacecraft on Mars in 21 years -- an electronic signal told scientists the Pathfinder had made a pinpoint landing.

"All indications so far have been very, very good," Flight Director Rob Manning said. There were shouts of joy in the mission control room at the lab as the craft ended an epic, 309-million mile (497 million km) journey.
"We're down," a delighted Manning shouted. His announcement shortly after 10 a.m. PDT (1700 GMT) was greeted with cheering and clapping as team members hugged each other.

The cheers started when Manning said the cruise module that carried the craft to Mars had separated from the entry vehicle and grew to a crescendo when he announced that the pyramid-shaped spacecraft appeared to have landed on its base.
In landing on the Red Planet, Pathfinder set a number of firsts.
* It was the first spacecraft to land on a planet without orbiting it.
* It was the first to deploy a parachute at a supersonic speed of 1,000 mph (1,600 kph).
* It was the first to use airbags, similar but larger to those used in automobiles, to cushion the impact of a landing.

When the six-wheeled rover starts its exploration, probably late on Friday or on Saturday, buggy "drivers" Brian Cooper, Howard Eisen and Andy Mishkin will become the envy of anyone who has ever played with a radio-operated remote-controlled toy car. The rover is also a "smart buggy," able to detect and avoid rocks bigger than itself.

The crew of the U.S. space shuttle Columbia, orbiting Earth on a 16-day science mission, also applauded the news of the Pathfinder landing. "That's great news," said shuttle skipper Jim Halsell. "Exciting stuff."
In an interview with CNN International, Halsell and his crew said they were ready to sign up for the first manned mission to Mars.
Flight controllers in Houston planned to beam the first images from the Mars probe to the shuttle later in the day.
